content_html:
By: Nicholas Grous and Austin Koring

In Part 1, we explained how Meta is already earning a return on AI through its advertising business. Now, we turn to the company’s rising capital expenditures (CapEx) and the infrastructure behind them. If AI is already working, why does Meta plan to spend roughly $135 billion in 2026, and how could that investment continue to generate returns?

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support our work.

The answer starts with the growing role of AI across Meta’s products. Meta AI, advertising, creative tools, business messaging, search, and smart glasses all require more training and inference as their models improve and usage expands. Serving those products to more than 3.5 billion people each day requires an enormous amount of compute, making it expensive to operate at Meta’s scale.

The Silicon Stack Is the Proof

Meta’s silicon strategy is focused on getting the right chip at the right cost.

Like a shipping network, different packages require different modes of transportation. Some packages require planes, while others are better handled by trucks or vans. Meta is taking the same approach to compute.

Nvidia graphics processing units GPUs handle frontier model training and the most demanding inference workloads. AMD adds capacity for large-scale inference. Meta’s custom Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), Meta Training and Inference Accelerator (MTIA), is designed for the repetitive ranking and recommendation workloads that run billions of times a day across its apps.

Using premium GPUs for every task would work, but it would be expensive and inefficient. Meta reserves the most advanced chips for workloads that require maximum performance and moves predictable, high-volume work onto cheaper, specialized hardware. On production recommendation workloads, Meta has reported approximately 44% lower total cost of ownership for MTIA than GPUs. This strategy was pioneered by hyperscalers like Amazon, which developed Graviton central processing units (CPUs) and custom networking chips to lower the cost of operating Amazon Web Services (AWS) at scale. The upfront research and development investment is substantial, making custom silicon practical only for companies operating at Meta’s scale.

Furthermore, Meta’s size makes owning infrastructure more attractive than renting it. Training the Llama 3.1 model family required a cumulative 39.3 million H100 GPU-hours across its 8-billion, 70-billion, and 405-billion-parameter models. At an illustrative public-cloud price of approximately $4 per GPU-hour, the cloud-equivalent training cost would have been about $157 million. Deploying the models creates additional, ongoing inference costs as users and developers generate prompts. Owning its infrastructure allows Meta to operate below public-cloud pricing, shift predictable inference to custom silicon, and reserve premium GPUs for frontier training and the most demanding workloads. MTIA lowers compute costs, improving the economics of Meta's existing AI workloads and making it cheaper to run larger models across more products and users. Lastly, at Meta’s scale, owning infrastructure ensures access to compute that would be difficult, if not impossible, to secure from third-party providers. Now, that same infrastructure may create a second monetization opportunity.

Compute May Become Meta’s Next Business

Meta is reportedly building a cloud business to sell its excess AI compute to outside customers and has introduced Muse Spark 1.1 through a paid model Application Programming Interface (API), giving developers access to one of its proprietary models. Infrastructure originally built for Meta’s own products could increasingly generate revenue from third parties.

Without external monetization, Meta’s infrastructure earns a return indirectly by making its products more useful and its advertising business more productive. With external monetization, some part of that same infrastructure could generate revenue directly. Based on our estimates, the company could operate ~28 gigawatts of AI compute capacity by 2030. We estimate ~9 gigawatts will remain dedicated to Meta’s core products, including advertising and recommendation systems, while another 15 gigawatts could support AI products that Meta monetizes itself, such as APIs and AI services. Our revenue forecast assumes Meta resells only one fifth of that monetizable capacity, or roughly 3.8 gigawatts, to external customers.

According to our Economics of a Gigawatt work, a single gigawatt of GB200-class AI capacity could support ~$14 billion in annual revenue if the owner simply rents the GPUs. Under those assumptions, the operating margin would be near 39%, roughly in line with mature cloud infrastructure margins. If that same gigawatt is used for inference, meaning running AI models and selling the output as tokens rather than renting the chips directly, the revenue potential could be closer to $35 billion. A blended estimate of $20 billion per gigawatt is a reasonable midpoint for sizing the opportunity, which may prove conservative if demand for frontier AI infrastructure continues to push rental pricing higher, as recent capacity agreements with Anthropic and Google suggest.

Selling capacity to outside customers would help Meta spread the cost of infrastructure it is already building for its own products. Unlike traditional cloud providers, Meta built this infrastructure to improve its own advertising and AI products first. External monetization would be a second return on an asset base that was already generating value internally.

The Capex Debate Has Changed

Will $135 billion of infrastructure spend ever generate an adequate return? After the progress described in Part 1, we think there are now two answers. The first is already visible, with AI improving Meta’s products, increasing advertiser returns, and making its core business more valuable.

The second is only beginning to emerge. If Meta successfully commercializes part of its infrastructure through hosted models or compute services, the same assets supporting its products today could support a second business line tomorrow.

For the first time, Meta’s AI infrastructure could lower its own AI costs while generating revenue from outside customers.
